title: The Unicorn Rests in a Garden (from the Unicorn Tapestries)
medium: Wool warp with wool, silk, silver, and gilt wefts

altText: A large woven tapestry of a white unicorn sitting inside a small round fence in a field thick with flowers, with a fruit tree beside it.

context: A tapestry from the Unicorn Tapestries, designed in a French style and woven in the Southern Netherlands about 1495–1505, now at The Cloisters. It is often called The Unicorn in Captivity. It shows a unicorn resting in an enclosed garden, surrounded by flowers and plants.

descriptions.k: A white unicorn rests in a garden. A little fence goes around it. Flowers cover the ground. A tree grows beside it. This big picture is made from thread. How many flowers can you find?
descriptions.g12: This big woven picture is called a tapestry. It was made over 500 years ago. A white unicorn rests inside a small round fence in a garden full of flowers. A tree grows nearby. Weavers made the picture from wool, silk, and shiny silver and gold threads. Which flowers can you find?
descriptions.g35: This tapestry was woven between 1495 and 1505 in the Southern Netherlands from a French design. It is the last of the seven Unicorn Tapestries at The Cloisters and is often called The Unicorn in Captivity. A unicorn rests inside a low fence, in a field of flowers, with a tree nearby. Weavers used wool, silk, and threads of silver and gilt. Look for the plants. Why might the weavers have filled the ground with so many different flowers?
descriptions.g68: The Unicorn Rests in a Garden, often called The Unicorn in Captivity, is part of the Unicorn Tapestries, designed in a French style and woven in the Southern Netherlands around 1495–1505. A unicorn sits within a circular fence beside a fruit-bearing tree, set against a field of many flowers, a style often called millefleurs, meaning a thousand flowers. Wool, silk, and silver and gilt threads give the surface a rich glow. Is the unicorn captive or at rest, and what details support each reading?
descriptions.g910: Often called The Unicorn in Captivity, this tapestry of about 1495–1505 was woven in the Southern Netherlands from a French design and is the last in the Unicorn Tapestries series. The unicorn sits within a fence in a dense field of flowers, with a fruit tree beside it. Scholars have proposed many readings: Christian symbolism, a courtly image of love or marriage, or a more general reference to nature, with its meaning debated. The weavers' rich surface of wool, silk, and metal threads adds status. How do the details support or complicate a single reading?
descriptions.g1112: The Unicorn Rests in a Garden, long known as The Unicorn in Captivity, closes the Unicorn Tapestries series. Designed in a French style and woven in the Southern Netherlands around 1495–1505, it shows a unicorn enclosed by a fence beside a fruit tree, within a field of many flowers. Interpretations include Christian allegory, marriage symbolism, and nature imagery, and the original patron and meaning remain debated. Its ambiguity, a captive that looks content, invites both formal and symbolic analysis. What evidence supports each interpretation, and how far should we trust symbolic readings of a luxury object with an unknown commission?

teacherNote.context: The seventh of the Unicorn Tapestries at The Cloisters, woven about 1495–1505 and often called The Unicorn in Captivity. The series includes hunting scenes; this panel shows a unicorn resting in a fenced garden.
directions: Have students identify five plants or flowers and sketch them, then discuss why weavers included so many.
Ask students to argue whether the unicorn is captive or at rest, citing visible details.
Compare with The Unicorn Purifies Water in the archive and discuss how each scene organizes its space.
